client: I've been really struggling since I got laid off from my tech job back in February — the financial pressure has been building up and I honestly don't know how much longer I can keep it together. Every time I try to sit down and update my resume, I just freeze up and end up closing the laptop without doing anything. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything practical, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a really heavy weight right now — the financial stress, the uncertainty, and then hitting that wall every time you try to take action must feel exhausting and frustrating. That freezing moment when you open the laptop is actually really meaningful to explore, because it often points to some powerful thoughts or fears happening just beneath the surface. What do you notice going through your mind in those seconds right before you close the laptop?

client: Honestly, it's like this rush of thoughts all at once — stuff like "what if I send this out and nobody responds" or "what if they can see I've been out of work this long and just write me off." And underneath that there's this louder voice saying maybe I just wasn't as good at my job as I thought I was, and getting laid off kind of proved it. I slam the laptop shut before I even have to face that possibility, I think.
therapist: That takes real courage to name — especially that deeper fear that the layoff was somehow proof of your worth, because that's a painful story to carry around. In CBT we'd call that a "hot thought," and it's worth gently challenging: a layoff in the tech industry, especially in the wave of cuts since 2022, is driven by budget decisions and market forces, not a performance review of your value as a person. What actual evidence from your time in that job — moments you solved a problem, helped a teammate, delivered something you were proud of — might push back against that story?

client: I mean, yeah, there were good moments — I led a migration project last year that actually came in under budget, and my manager at the time told me I'd saved the team probably two months of work. But here's the thing, when I try to hold onto that memory right now, it just feels distant, like it happened to a different person, and my brain immediately counters with "well, if you were so great, why did they pick you to let go." I get what you're saying about market forces, and logically I know layoffs were everywhere, but that logical part doesn't seem to have much power over the part that's convinced I was the weak link.
therapist: That gap you're describing — where logic knows one thing but the gut feeling insists on another — is so common and so frustrating, and it doesn't mean the logical part is wrong, it just means the emotional belief has had a lot more practice and repetition. That migration project isn't a small thing; leading something complex under budget and saving your team two months of work is concrete, observable evidence that directly contradicts the "weak link" story. I'm curious — if a close friend described that same accomplishment to you and then said "but I must have deserved to get laid off," what would you actually say back to them?

client: I'd probably tell them that's ridiculous, that one project like that shows real skill and the layoffs were happening everywhere. But when I try to turn that same logic on myself it just feels hollow, like I'm reciting something I'm supposed to believe rather than actually believing it. I guess I can see what you're doing with that question, and it's a fair point, but I don't know how to make that compassion feel real when it's directed at me instead of someone else.
therapist: What you just identified is actually a really important insight — that gap between knowing something and *feeling* it is real, and it's not a flaw in your thinking, it's just that self-compassion is genuinely a skill that takes practice, not a switch you can flip. One small thing that sometimes helps bridge that gap is literally writing to yourself as if you were that friend — not to recite the "right" answer, but to see if a different voice on the page feels any less hollow than the one in your head. Would you be open to trying something like that this week, even just a few sentences, and noticing what comes up?

client: I'm willing to try it, but I'm already imagining sitting down to write it and just staring at a blank page feeling stupid, like I'm writing a letter to myself is going to fix the fact that I still have no income coming in. There's also this part of me that worries I'll write it and it'll still feel hollow, and then I'll have proof that even therapy exercises don't work for me, which honestly sounds worse than not trying. I don't know, maybe I'm just looking for reasons to avoid it the same way I avoid the resume.
therapist: That fear of trying and still feeling nothing — like it would become evidence against yourself — is actually the same protective move as closing the laptop, and it makes a lot of sense that your mind goes there. But notice what you just did: you caught yourself looking for reasons to avoid, which is a really honest and self-aware thing to see in real time, and that's not nothing. What if we made the exercise almost impossible to fail — not a heartfelt letter, just two or three sentences, and the only goal is to notice what it feels like to try, not to feel better afterward?

client: Okay, two or three sentences feels a lot less overwhelming than what I was picturing, and I think I can at least attempt that without feeling like I'm setting myself up for some big failure. I guess my worry is that even that small version will somehow get tangled up with the resume avoidance — like I'll sit down to write the sentences and then feel guilty that I'm not using that time to actually apply for jobs instead. It's hard to justify anything that feels like "working on myself" when the practical problem of paying rent is still just sitting there.
therapist: That guilt makes complete sense given the real financial pressure you're under, and it's not irrational — rent is concrete and urgent in a way that two sentences on a page doesn't feel like it is. But here's something worth considering: the freezing at the laptop isn't a time management problem, it's a belief problem, and if those three sentences start to loosen that "weak link" story even slightly, they might actually be the thing that makes the resume feel more approachable. What would it mean for the practical job search if you could sit down at the laptop without that wave of dread hitting you first?

client: Honestly, if I could open the laptop without that immediate dread, I think I'd actually get something done — even just updating the dates or tweaking a bullet point would feel like progress instead of this all-or-nothing paralysis. I can see the logic of what you're saying, that the freezing is the real obstacle and not just laziness or bad time management, and part of me wants to believe that. But there's still this nagging voice saying "what if you fix the dread and the resume still doesn't get any responses" — like I'm not sure I can handle putting in the effort and then facing silence from employers on top of everything else.
therapist: You're in a slightly calmer place right now than earlier, and that moment of clarity — "I'd actually get something done" — is worth holding onto, because you just described what's possible when the dread isn't running the show. That fear of silence from employers is real and worth taking seriously, but it's a future problem, and right now your mind is using it as a reason to not even begin — which means you're experiencing the pain of rejection without any of the actual chances it might go differently. What would "handling" silence from employers look like for you — not perfectly, but just well enough to keep going?

client: I think "just well enough to keep going" would probably look like allowing myself to feel disappointed for a day and then trying to remind myself it's a numbers game, not a verdict on me — though I honestly don't know if I'd actually be able to do that in the moment. The thing is, I've been so isolated since the layoff that there's nobody around to help me shake off a rejection, and I think that silence from employers would just echo in a really lonely way. I don't have the buffer of, like, a work community anymore, and that scares me more than I realized until just now.
therapist: That realization you just landed on — that the isolation might actually be the deeper wound underneath all of this — feels really significant, and it took courage to let yourself see it mid-conversation. The layoff didn't just take income, it took your daily community, the people who knew your work and reflected your competence back to you, and that's a real loss that deserves to be named as such. Who in your life, even someone you've drifted from a little, might be someone you could start to rebuild even a small sense of connection with right now?

client: There's a former colleague, Marcus, who I actually got along with really well and we said we'd grab coffee after the layoffs but I never followed through — I think I was too ashamed to let him see me still floundering months later. The idea of reaching out feels embarrassing, like I'd have to explain why I waited so long and admit that I haven't landed anything yet. I don't want the first thing he knows about my life after the job to be that I'm still struggling.
therapist: It's tender and vulnerable to sit with that shame, and it makes sense that it's kept you from reaching out — but it's worth noticing that the story you're telling yourself is that Marcus would see you as a failure, when the evidence you have is that he's someone you genuinely connected with and who wanted to stay in touch. Most people don't think "why did they wait so long" when an old colleague reaches out — they just feel glad to hear from them. What do you imagine Marcus's actual reaction would be if you sent him a simple message saying you've been meaning to reach out and would still love to grab that coffee?

client: Honestly, if I'm being fair to Marcus, he'd probably just say "yeah, finally, let's do it" and not make a big deal out of the gap at all — he was never the type to be weird about that stuff. But I think the problem is less about what he'd actually say and more about sitting across from him at a coffee shop and him asking "so how's the job search going" and having to say out loud that it's been months and nothing yet. That feels like the moment I'd want to disappear, and I'm not sure I'm ready to be that exposed with someone who knew me when I was doing well.
therapist: You already know Marcus well enough to predict he'd be warm and low-key about the gap — that's actually really useful information your own mind just gave you. And that moment you're dreading, having to say "it's been months and nothing yet," is painful partly because it feels like a confession of failure, but what if it's also just... the truth, spoken to someone who already respects you? What would it feel like to let one person who knew you at your best also know you during a hard stretch — not as a collapse of your image, but as a sign that you trust him?
